stories.title_en: Deceiving the Provincial Education Commissioner with Fake Silver

paragraphs.en: Whenever the Provincial Education Commissioner goes on tour, crooks from every quarter gather and follow him, hunting for rich men’s sons who want to buy influence. They offer openings of every kind, hoping to cheat them. If one pitch does not take, another gang comes along with a different angle; every year some fall for it. But the families who are cheated are too ashamed to tell anyone, so the next people walk into the same trap.

There was an education commissioner, scrupulously fair in his examinations, who took no private requests. Suddenly a con man claimed he could channel directly to the commissioner; no one believed him. The con man said, “This commissioner has opened a private door himself. He hates it when people send introductions through intermediaries. Only those who deal with him face-to-face succeed every time—people just don’t dare. If you truly mean to do it, all you need is ready money; he’ll take it in person, and success is as good as guaranteed.” Zhao Jia asked, “Where do we present it?” The con man said, “Wait until he leaves the hall. First use a petition listing such-and-such county, so-and-so, so many taels of silver, asking to be admitted to the school. If he agrees in person, then hand over the silver; if he doesn’t, the silver remains in my hands—what can he do to me?” Zhao Jia said, “I want to stand beside you and watch for myself.” The con man said, “Of course you’ll watch for yourself. The second gate of the education commissioner’s office has a crack an inch wide; peeking from outside you can see straight into the hall—watch as you wish.” Zhao Jia said, “If the commissioner will take the silver with his own hands, I’ll dare to go in.” He wrote a petition and wrapped two hundred taels in a handkerchief as one packet.

That afternoon they went out and waited in front of the commissioner's office. The con man said, "I need two packets of silver to get through the gate." Jia paid him. As the session was about to end, the con man took the silver and the petition and slipped into the hall, telling Jia, "The moment they seal the gate, come look through the crack." After the commissioner left the hall, Jia looked through the crack in the second gate and saw a man still in gauze cap and round-collared robe come out. The con man first held the petition high; a yamen attendant took it in. The commissioner opened it, looked it over, and tucked it into his sleeve. The con man then held a packet of silver high; the commissioner glanced at the attendant; the attendant took up the silver. The commissioner glanced at it and turned; the attendant followed him in, carrying the silver packet. The con man hurried to the second gate and said through the door, "It's done, it's done! Did you see?" Jia said, "I saw it myself; he did take it with his own hands." The con man said, "I can't go out tonight; you and I will have to sleep on either side of the gate." Jia said, "If the business is settled, going without supper is fine."

The next morning, when the early gate opened, the con man and Jia went out together and visited Jia’s shop to celebrate his success. Jia hosted a lavish feast. The con man said, "Once you secure your winnings, you must reward me generously." Jia replied, "Adding an extra thank-you gift is the fixed rule; I won’t add anything beyond that, nor will I subtract anything." Let this serve as a warning against trusting crooks.

On the day the results were announced, the victim's name was nowhere to be found. The swindler had vanished. Only then did they realize that the way the silver had been taken earlier was because this swindler had first colluded with the night-duty yamen men to stage a fake official.

Looking from the second gate into the hall, though you can see it yourself, the distance is still great—how can you see clearly? So they fell for this swindle without realizing it. If an official were truly accepting silver personally, why come out in full dress? Why present a petition in the hall? Why hand over silver in the hall? Couldn't the petition be passed privately? Besides, the hall has staff on duty—is that a place to accept silver in secret? This rustic rich man did not understand official protocol, so he took seeing with his own eyes as proof; he did not realize that letting you see with your own eyes was exactly how they cheated you.

stories.title_en: The Swindler's Seal: A Trick in a Retired Official's Private Quarters

paragraphs.en: Rich man Qian Yi wanted to buy his son a place in the school. Innkeeper Sun Bing intended to cheat him and said, "There is a retired official named Li here who was once a colleague of the education commissioner; the two are very close. If we speak up for one candidate, we can certainly secure admission. Let me try discussing it with him." Qian Yi said, "All right." Sun Bing went to a craftsman's shop, saw two identical chests, bought one for three qian, and paid a deposit of two fen to reserve the second, telling them, "In a moment I'll bring someone to buy it; he will pay another three qian—do not swap it for a different one." He also bought two identical locks. Then he gave a chest and lock to Official Li's servant: "Weigh out two hundred taels of stones, put them in the chest, lock it from the outside, and place it in your master's room. Shortly I will bring someone asking your master to speak for school admission, bringing two hundred taels of good silver for you to seal. You take in the chest with the silver, swap it for the chest with the stones, then split this silver with me." Li's servant agreed: "All right."

Sun Bing brought Li’s servant and told Qian Yi: “I met Lord Li in person. He said this is easy: have the ready silver shown to his servant, checked and locked, sent to his house to be sealed, then return the silver chest to me while giving him the key to keep. Once he passes the examination and enters the academy, the original silver will serve as his thanks; the chest must not be opened or swapped.” Qian Yi said, “I’ll borrow a chest from your place.” Sun Bing replied, “I have a new lock; you can buy the chest at a shop.” He led one of Qian’s men, paid three qian, and bought it. With Li’s servant and Sun Bing watching, Qian Yi verified two hundred taels of silver, placed them in the chest, and locked it securely.

Sun Bing carried the silver chest with Qian Yi to Official Li’s house, requesting a sealing strip. Official Li feigned illness and sat in a room to the left of the hall. Li’s servant held the chest at the doorway: "The silver has been verified against the mark; we only need one sealing strip." Official Li replied, "Since it’s been checked clearly, give it back for him to keep, and come fetch the sealing strip." The servant took the chest out again, then brought out a sealing strip and sealed all three sides before them. Qian Yi handed over the key to Li’s servant. Sun Bing carried the silver chest back and gave it to Qian Yi to store away; everyone thought the matter perfectly secure.

When the results were posted, Qian Yi's son had no name on the list. Sun Bing said, "It didn't work; the silver is still here. Pack up and head home quickly, lest Li's people come asking for sedan-chair fees." Qian Yi, disappointed, headed home dejected. Halfway there he called a carpenter to open the lock and look: all stones. Shocked, he went back and made a scene at the inn: "How did you collude to cheat me?" Sun Bing said, "I did the business with you face to face; where was the cheat? If the three of us had opened the chest together, you could still blame the Li household; now after half a day's travel you opened the chest in private—how would I know whether inside was silver or stone?" Qian Yi knew perfectly well that Sun and Li had cheated him together, but there was no proof; he figured the silver would be hard to recover, so he only cursed the innkeeper roundly and headed home. Take this as a lesson: do not trust retired officials.

Note: Two chests of identical pattern are naturally hard to distinguish. Yet applying a seal only requires doing so on the outside; why carry them inside to report and then request the seal? Had the victim reported it to the magistrate at the time, investigating the shop that sold the chests and asking why two were alike might have revealed that Sun Bing first bought one, then arranged for another to be purchased. With a clear-sighted official, the package-swap swindle could have been exposed from this.

Hao Tianguang of Jianning Prefecture hailed from a distinguished and immensely wealthy family, owning several estates stocked largely with white rice. At the time, rice prices in Jianning were low; his steward Luo Wu learned that prices in the provincial capital were soaring and invited his master to take two servants along, loading over ten boats of rice for sale there. Just then, Chief Examiner Lord Wang issued orders to examine students from both Yanping and Jianning prefectures, issuing proclamations for the civil service exams for young scholars. Once the rice was on board, a guest accompanied by two servants arrived to book passage to the capital. Seated at leisure on the boat, they asked what his business was. He replied, "I have come from Lord Wang's household to deliver a letter." Later, the conversation turned to securing favors through connections. Tianguang had his eldest son taking the exam; the talk suited him well. However, since Chief Examiner Wang had conducted the previous examinations very fairly, with no private loopholes, he did not quite dare to believe it.

At the provincial capital, the crook took his leave: "Lord Wang has a son in the school; they are sure to look at papers together. I'll try talking about your honorable house; if he agrees, I'll come out and bring you the yes; if I don't come out, the matter isn't on, and there will be no further word." Tianguang said, "Right." He secretly sent a servant to track where the crook went; indeed he went into the Education Commissioner's yamen. After several days he came out: "It's arranged. Verify the silver, hide it in my leather case, add a sealing strip outside; the silver stays in your own keeping. After the name is on the list for school, you hand the leather case of silver over to me." Tianguang thought, "Though the silver is verified, I still keep it—what's wrong with that?" He followed the instructions and verified it, not knowing what method this crook had. Tianguang clearly put the silver in and locked it himself; the crook only added one sealing strip and left, then added: "Tonight the young master may slip out; I'll look it over with him, and the matter will be fine." They waited several nights; he did not come. Tianguang opened the leather case: all bricks and stones; the silver had been cheated away. Let this serve as a warning: when sealing silver, guard against a swap.

Note: Buying a school place, buying a stipend, even buying the juren degree—this happens everywhere, every year, and Jianning Prefecture has been cheated over and over, worse than anywhere else. The people of Jian commandery are rich with much wealth, and their nature is light and flighty. Though they have been cheated again and again, those who follow up to buy still do not stop; so sharps on the road often treat the Jianning exams as a lucrative business. The method of sealing silver, especially, people still cannot see through to this day. Clearly, you seal the silver together, it is given back for you to keep, and after the crook leaves, you open it—all bricks and stones. Some think there is a method of making silver vanish. How miraculous—even the wisest can hardly guard against it! Only see this clearly; not believing is best. If you urgently want to buy entry, don't seal silver; take a name on the posted list as the settlement. If you only believe his leaked reports, even if you see the golden list three or four times, you still must not hand over silver; only then can you guard against being cheated out of it.

stories.title_en: Sealing Silver in an Empty House, Then a Staged Robbery

paragraphs.en: Swindles take many forms; yet in the path of official advancement, so many rush headlong that the number of victims is vast. Swindlers often say: only an empty name can cheat one out of solid profit; only hollow reputation can earn real goods. For those seeking office, their hunger for fame is so intense that they throw down heavy sums without pausing to consider, thus falling into the swindler's trap without noticing.

A wealthy family's son sought to scheme his way into the academy; the steward he brought was extremely capable. They traveled to the provincial capital for the examination and lodged at an inn, instructing the steward to find a way through. Within days, various people offering connections arrived one after another. The steward observed their conduct, traced their backgrounds, and found their words inconsistent with their actions, their tracks unclear, and many colluding with the innkeeper. He rejected them all, refusing to believe their lies. Later, a crook dressed as a servant, slow of speech and rustic in manner, claimed he followed a dismissed country official who had old ties with the Chief Examiner and had come here to mooch off them. He led the steward to see the official, who indeed looked like a poor minor official. They settled on a price for one admission to the academy; even a hundred taels as a bribe he would discuss, provided it was ready silver, sealed at his inn. The steward said, "Seal it at my inn." The official replied, "The matter must be discreet; your inn has too many people, making it inconvenient if word spreads. Down below there is an empty house belonging to Scholar Gu. I intended to lodge there before, but borrowing furnishings was inconvenient, so I moved here. You and my little servant can seal the deal there; that is most secure." The steward insisted the official come to their inn to witness the sealing. The official said, "If you still doubt, I have only one little servant; you may send as many people as you like to seal together." The steward replied, "Outsiders must not know; I will only go with my master." Indeed, only the rustic servant was present. They brought out the silver and verified its weight and quality. Suddenly several crooks burst in: "You are buying a xiucai degree! We'll take you and report it!" They beat the three men down and robbed all the silver.

The rustic servant got up, putting on a distressed look. The steward rose, took his hand, and said, “Don’t worry; this silver isn’t much. Come to my inn with me, and we’ll seal it again.” The servant refused to go. The rich son said, “The matter has already gone wrong; how can we do it again?” The steward replied, “I have a way.” He forced the servant to return, while simultaneously telling the rich son to pack up and head home quickly. The steward hired men from the inn, passed himself off as a scholar, had them lock themselves together with the rustic servant, and sent them to the county yamen, where he verbally accused them of being robbed. The magistrate said, “You shouldn’t have bought into the scholar-official class; both giver and receiver are guilty. Besides, being robbed by crooks—what does that have to do with a retired official’s servant?” The steward said, “The robbers were this crook’s accomplices. Only thoroughly investigate where this silver came from; I am willing to have it recovered for the government, and I am also willing to be heavily fined, sharing the same crime as this crook.” The magistrate then sent people to summon the retired official, but he had already fled. The magistrate declared, “This is indeed a crook,” and ordered harsh torture. The servant-crook could not bear the punishment and agreed to repay half. After recovering that amount, the steward again petitioned, demanding full recovery and willing to accept joint exile to a garrison station. The servant-crook would rather die than name his accomplices; tortured repeatedly, nothing more could be recovered. Thus, the servant-crook was sentenced to penal servitude, while the steward received only beating and was released. This serves as a warning: when sealing silver, guard against robbery.

Note: Although the steward was capable, he ultimately fell victim to the swindler's theft. However, after the robbery, if he were willing to arrest the swindler and accept joint liability for the crime, he could eventually recover half the money, leaving the swindler with no profit. If it had been the rich son himself, he would surely refuse to share the blame with the swindler; once robbed, there would be nothing to be done. Some ask: What if the steward claimed to be a scholar? How would the official test him? Answer: A man who secures influence through connections is already a master of the game; why would the official need to test him? Even if he failed the exam, it wouldn't matter.

stories.title_en: Impersonating a Favor-Seeking Guest to Solicit Exam Bribes

paragraphs.en: Education Commissioner Jian was renowned for his integrity and clear judgment. During the student renewal examinations, a favor-seeking visitor arrived and lodged in the monks' quarters at Kaiming Temple. The next day, a swindler arrived with three servants and took lodgings there as well. Inside the temple they exchanged courtesy calls, and the swindler claimed to be a relative of the county magistrate who had also come to solicit favors. Outwardly, he flaunted splendid robes and caps, with a retinue even grander than the other's, frequently coming and going through the temple under official canopies. Students who saw him often mistook him, saying, "This is the Education Commissioner's hometown relative." When they saw Commissioner Jian's real relative return a courtesy call and invite him for wine, the swindler tagged along with the genuine visitor while secretly borrowing his name on the outside to deceive people. Commissioner Jian was a strict and upright official, and within a few days the genuine favor-seeker was sent on his way, leaving only the swindler at the temple. His outside accomplices deliberately spread word everywhere: "The Education Commissioner's hometown relative is staying at such-and-such temple." The rumor circulated widely among the candidates; many who wished to buy a place in the examination were eager to pay, yet lacked a reliable person to handle the silver. Behind the scenes, the swindler colluded with clerks and runners from the Education Commissioner's yamen, having them come forward so the silver could be sealed and deposited at their homes. Since people already believed he was the genuine relative, and since official yamen staff were involved, what was there to worry about in sealing the silver at their houses? The swindler announced that he could secure ten places at three hundred taels each. With so many candidates competing eagerly, the quota of ten was filled within days. On the appointed day, the silver—three thousand taels in all—was openly checked, sealed, and deposited at the various clerks' and runners' homes; behind the scenes, the gang divided the spoils at once.

But they thought: later, if they have no name to give, they cannot answer anyone—and how will they get the silver away? So they hired someone to go to the Education Office and report: "Clerks and runners so-and-so of the yamen, together with an outside traveling swindler, solicited so many taels from students, sealed at so-and-so’s homes." Jian accepted the complaint, issued a plain warrant to seize the traveling swindler with utmost haste; the Autumn Wind Swindler then used the chance to flee. Then they seized the yamen clerks and runners, put them to the squeezers and presses; none would confess; each was beaten thirty strokes and dismissed. They sent men to search the yamen staff’s homes. Anyone named as having bought their position, hearing their tracks were exposed, feared being named and arrested, scattered in all directions, fled back to their home counties, abandoned the silver, and dared not come ask. Thus the swindler could enjoy in peace the silver he’d split. The clerks and runners, though dismissed, had no stolen goods that could be proven; later they gradually schemed their way back in. They only suffered squeezing and beating for a time; using punishment on yamen staff is also just like putting on a play; and what they got was more than enough to repay the loss! Let this serve as a warning against trusting the Autumn Wind Swindler.

Note: This crook claimed to be the education commissioner’s hometown relative. Since the commissioner had already visited and invited him to drink, he truly seemed a hometown relative. Besides, clerks and runners all held official posts, shielding him—who would suspect? They didn’t know the real relative had departed, and this was merely someone borrowing his name. Those yamen men care only for profit; having collected so much, what did they care about enduring a few dozen strokes of the cane? Moreover, the silver they paid to buy their posts remains intact; even if dismissed, how could that serve as punishment? People today say yamen runners know the law; they fail to realize that those who abuse the law are precisely those who know it best. Only walk on solid ground, do solid things, and win true fame through true learning. Do not sprout hopes of lucky breaks, nor plot to buy influence—how then could swindles take hold? Those who are cheated are all lazy, unworthy students who bring disaster upon themselves.

stories.title_en: Silver Left with an Innkeeper, Who Steals It and Flees

paragraphs.en: Three crooks in a gang cheated out of three hundred taels together but refused to split them; instead, they pooled the silver to set up a front for a bigger swindle. First, they sent one man across the province to a prefecture two days from the capital, where he spent seventy taels to buy a house with an earthen storehouse inside and opened shop premises outside the wall as a guest inn. Another fifty taels went toward marrying a wife, buying a maid, and purchasing a male slave. They kept several tens of taels on hand for household expenses. Seeing that the inn had a family, servants, and abundant provisions, many travelers chose to stay there. This prefecture was near the provincial capital; in previous years, when the provincial examinations were held elsewhere, students from neighboring prefectures were often transferred here for joint exams to make travel easier. Consequently, wealthy students selecting an inn invariably stayed at this one.

In the sixth month of a Renzi year, with the exam deadline pressing, students from two outer prefectures were again summoned here for selection. Three xiucai from Jian commandery resided at our inn, all men of great wealth. One day, a visiting scholar, impressive in appearance and neatly dressed, moored his boat outside the city wall and entered the inn. He asked the innkeeper in secret: "Do you know among the exam xiucai any from wealthy families?" The innkeeper replied: "The three in my inn are all rich; why do you ask?" The guest said: "I have a good matter to discuss with them." The innkeeper asked: "What good matter? Why not tell me?" The guest replied: "You are not versed in this matter; I can only speak with the xiucai." The innkeeper went out and told the three: "This gentleman asked which of the exam xiucai is the richest; he has a good matter to share. When I asked what it was, he refused to say. You gentlemen should try asking him." The three went in, exchanged courtesies, and asked: "You asked about rich families; our households each possess ten thousand taels; what good matter is there?" The guest said: "Would you gentlemen be willing to negotiate the arrangement?" The three replied: "We are all willing to negotiate; what channel do you have, brother?" The guest said: "I cannot act on my own, nor do I know a channel. But if you truly wish to negotiate, each prepare one thousand taels, come to this inn, verify the silver and seal it, then hand it back for you to keep; a path will be pointed out." The three agreed to fetch the silver from home in four days to verify; the visiting scholar departed. The three secretly sent someone to follow him; they saw him board a boat where only one servant remained. They reported this; the three rejoiced: "This must be an associate of the chief examiner; he can be trusted." The innkeeper came out and asked: "What did you just discuss?" The three replied: "This is not yet certain; if the matter succeeds, we will ensure you are greatly elevated."

Four days later, the servants from all three households arrived with the silver. The visiting scholar came on schedule to inquire, and each of the three scholars replied, "The silver is all ready." The visitor said, "Tonight let us verify it under bright light and seal it." The three scholars said, "There is a great deal of silver, which makes nighttime inconvenient; tomorrow let us go into the innkeeper's inner courtyard to verify it." The visitor said, "The innkeeper may not keep this matter confidential; sealing it in the outer guest rooms would be more discreet." The three scholars said, "Let us discuss it when the time comes tomorrow." The visitor took his leave. After supper, the innkeeper came out and said, "You gentlemen were discussing sealing silver with that visitor—traveling strangers are hard to guard against. These doors and walls are thin; if they bring a gang to rob you in the night, you must be on your guard. In my opinion, you should store the silver inside my house within the city gate while you keep watch outside; that will be completely secure." The three scholars agreed and entrusted all six leather chests of silver to the innkeeper's house. Concealing it from his wife and maid, the innkeeper slipped all the silver out through the back door and fled late at night with the gang of crooks. Before leaving, he merely instructed his wife: "Tomorrow, if the three scholars ask for me, just tell them I went out early to look for someone and will be back shortly."

The next day, the visiting scholar arrived in high spirits to weigh and verify the silver. The scholars said, "We gave the silver to the innkeeper for safekeeping; he went out early this morning and will be back shortly." They waited until noon, but the innkeeper did not return, so the visitor went back to his boat. In the afternoon, the visitor sent his servant to ask again, and once more they answered that the innkeeper had not yet returned. At noon on the third day, the scholars asked the innkeeper's wife for the leather chests, but she replied, "I have never seen any chests." When they went out to the riverbank to look for the visitor's boat, it too had vanished. They questioned the innkeeper's wife again, and she stubbornly insisted she knew nothing of the chests. She let them search the house as they pleased, yet not a trace was found. "Where did the innkeeper really go?" they demanded. The wife replied, "He left the night before last and told me to answer you this way." The three scholars were thrown into a panic.

By then these three crooks, having made off with the silver, were already out of the territory. At night they lodged at an inn. The innkeeper saw they came late, hefted the six cases—all heavy—and suspected they were thieves; he planned to gather people to seize them the next day. The three heard the stir; next morning before dawn they carried off only four cases and left two at the inn. The innkeeper became even more convinced they were thieves and reported them to the officials. The prefect opened the silver packets one by one; inside one seal was a contract document stating that so-and-so was buying a juren degree. The prefect summoned that student; he dared not admit it. The prefect lured him with sweet words until he confessed, whereupon he was thrown into jail. Later, he sought connections to settle the matter but was cheated out of another four hundred taels before they would refrain from reporting it to the commissioner. They also confiscated the innkeeper’s house, sold his wife and maid by official order, and recovered the thousand taels in the cases into the treasury. The four cases the crooks carried off luckily had no names on them, so those students were not cheated again. Thus the prefectural official was also a crook. Let this serve as a warning to innkeepers.

Note: An innkeeper with a family is the most reliable. If he agrees to store your silver, who wouldn't trust him? Yet who would guess that his wives and concubines were all purchased merely to play the part of the crook's accomplices? Once he has reaped a fat profit, he abandons them and departs, marrying new wives and concubines to enjoy great wealth. Even an innkeeper with dependents cannot be trusted—the perils of the road have reached such extremes! Why do people not stick to honest work, instead trusting crooks to gamble on dangerous paths?
